intro.title: How to use this module
intro.intro:
This is the full, first-pass postgraduate teaching text for the Vulvar Pathology lecture — not a condensed exam-revision sheet. Read each sub-topic in full before moving to Revision or Quiz: the goal here is complete understanding of the morphology, classification and clinical correlation, so that the single-best-answer questions built later from this same content are answered from comprehension rather than recall of an isolated fact. Where the lecture supplies a classification, a table, or a numeric threshold (FIGO stage, percentage risk of progression, margin distance), that exact wording and those exact numbers are preserved, because postgraduate exams test them precisely.

**Priority legend**
- **MUST-KNOW** — explicitly tested in the department's existing Google Forms quiz, or a named classification/staging system (VIN subtypes, FIGO stage) an examiner would expect verbatim.
- **HIGH-YIELD** — major content the lecture devotes substantial emphasis to; very likely to appear in some form.
- **SUPPORTING** — background, rarer entities, or supplementary detail that completes the picture but is less likely to be independently tested.

A few lines are marked **[CLARIFICATION]** — one-line additions of context the lecture assumes but does not spell out. Everything else below is drawn directly from the lecture.

---

subs.title: Surface anatomy and landmarks
subs.label: COURSE
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** The vulva is the female external genitalia, comprising the labia majora and labia minora, together with the mons pubis, clitoris and prepuce, the vestibule, and the perineum as surrounding landmarks. The **vestibule** is the "inner vulva" — it extends from **Hart's line** to the **hymen**. Four structures open into the vestibule: the **major vestibular (Bartholin) glands**, the **minor vestibular glands**, the **periurethral (Skene) glands**, and the **urethra**. The Bartholin ducts enter the vestibule posterolaterally, adjacent to the hymen, corresponding clinically to the **4 and 8 o'clock** positions — the site where a Bartholin cyst or abscess classically presents.

**[CLARIFICATION]** Hart's line is the mucocutaneous junction on the medial aspect of the labia minora that marks the transition from keratinized vulvar skin to the non-keratinized vestibular mucosa.

subs.title: Epithelial histology of the vulva
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** The vulva is covered by stratified squamous epithelium, but the type of keratinization differs by site.

**Morphology (microscopic):** The **labia majora** are lined by **keratinized** stratified squamous epithelium. The **vestibule and labia minora** are lined by **non-keratinized** squamous epithelium. In normal vulvar epithelium, the basal cell layer has a higher nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, and the cells mature gradually toward the surface. Unlike the cervix, **cytoplasmic glycogen and its associated perinuclear vacuoles are largely absent** in normal vulvar epithelium.

In contrast, epithelial dysplasia of the vulva (epithelial dysplasia/condyloma) typically distorts the normal architecture — seen as **acanthosis and papillary growth** — and characteristically shows **perinuclear vacuoles**, a finding that is **not normally seen in vulva** (unlike the cervix, where such vacuolation from glycogen is a normal finding). The presence of perinuclear vacuoles in vulvar epithelium is therefore an abnormal, HPV-related change, not a normal variant.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The single most important trap in this topic is the cervix/vulva contrast: glycogenated cells with perinuclear clearing are a normal koilocyte-mimicking feature of the normal cervix, but the same finding in the vulva is abnormal and should prompt consideration of HPV-related epithelial change.

**Image:** pic:vu012

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.11–12*

subs.title: Labia majora: dermis, adnexa, and interlabial glands
subs.label: COURSE
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Beneath the vulvar epithelium, the composition of the underlying tissue differs sharply between the labia majora and labia minora, and this difference is a recognized histologic discriminator between the two sites.

**Morphology (microscopic):** The tissue underlying the labia majora epithelium contains **collagen, adipose tissue, and adnexal structures**. **Sebaceous glands**, with or without associated hair follicles, are commonly identified at various levels within the labia majora; as elsewhere in the body, these sebaceous glands contain clear, vacuolated cytoplasm. Adnexal structures and adipose tissue are typically **absent in the labia minora** — a useful microscopic clue to site of origin when the anatomic label on a specimen is uncertain.

The sulcus between the labia majora and labia minora contains **mammary-like anogenital glands**. These glands are clinically important because they are the presumed origin of breast-like lesions arising in the vulva, such as fibroadenoma and hidradenoma papilliferum (covered fully in Section 5).

**Differential diagnosis:** A biopsy showing adipose tissue and adnexal (pilosebaceous) structures favors labial majora origin; their absence favors labia minora or vestibule.

subs.title: Bartholin gland and duct histology
subs.label: COURSE
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** The Bartholin (major vestibular / bulbourethral) gland complex has three histologically distinct components — the secretory acini, the small ducts near the acini, and the main excretory duct — each with a characteristic epithelial lining that is important for recognizing both the normal gland and its cystic or neoplastic transformations.

**Morphology (microscopic):** The **mucinous acini** are lined by small, cytologically bland, **pyknotic nuclei** with abundant **pale (blue-grey) cytoplasm**; the intervening stroma is typically densely collagenized. The **ductal epithelium located near the main acini** has a flattened appearance with scant cytoplasm, while the adjacent mucinous glands retain their abundant blue-grey cytoplasm. The **main Bartholin duct**, which enters the vulvar vestibule posterolaterally adjacent to the hymen, often has a **urothelial-type (transitional) epithelium**, with peripheral foci of mucinous-type glandular epithelium. This transitional epithelium closely resembles urothelium, and **cystic change may occur in these ducts**, producing a clinically apparent mass lesion (the Bartholin duct/gland cyst discussed in Section 4).

| Component | Histology |
|---|---|
| Acini | Mucinous cells, pale (blue-grey) cytoplasm, small bland pyknotic nuclei; densely collagenized stroma |
| Ducts near acini | Flattened epithelium, scant cytoplasm |
| Main duct | Urothelial-type (transitional) epithelium, ± peripheral mucinous foci |

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The main duct's transitional (urothelial-type) lining is easy to mistake for an incidental urothelial contaminant or for evidence of a different process; it is a normal finding at this specific site.

subs.title: Reaction-pattern classification of vulvar dermatoses
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Rather than being memorized as an unrelated list, vulvar inflammatory dermatoses are classified by the **histologic reaction pattern** they produce. This reaction-pattern framework is the organizing scheme the lecture uses for the whole of Section 2, and each dermatosis below maps onto one row of this table.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria:**

| Pattern | Examples |
|---|---|
| Spongiotic | Atopic dermatitis; allergic contact dermatitis; irritant contact dermatitis |
| Acanthotic (formerly "squamous cell hyperplasia") | Psoriasis; lichen simplex chronicus; primary (idiopathic); secondary (superimposed on lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, or other vulvar disease) |
| Lichenoid | Lichen sclerosus; lichen planus |
| Dermal homogenization / sclerosis | Lichen sclerosus |
| Vesiculobullous | Pemphigoid (cicatricial type); linear IgA disease |
| Acantholytic | Hailey–Hailey disease; Darier disease; papular genitocrural acantholysis |
| Granulomatous | Crohn disease; Melkersson–Rosenthal syndrome |
| Vasculopathic | Aphthous ulcers; Behçet disease; plasma cell vulvitis |

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** Lichen sclerosus is unusual in appearing in **two** reaction-pattern rows simultaneously — lichenoid (early) and dermal homogenization/sclerosis (established) — reflecting its evolution over time (see 2.5). The acanthotic pattern's older name, "squamous cell hyperplasia," is a historical synonym an examiner may use interchangeably with the current terminology.


**Image:** pic:vu020

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.20*

subs.title: Irritant contact dermatitis
subs.label: COURSE
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Irritant contact dermatitis is caused by direct skin injury, direct cytotoxic effects, or cutaneous inflammation resulting from contact with an irritant substance — it is not immune-mediated.

**Clinical features:** Typical irritants include **urine, soaps, detergents, antiseptics, and deodorants**. Clinically it presents as **well-defined erythematous papules and plaques**.

**Morphology (microscopic):** Falls under the spongiotic reaction pattern (see 2.1).

**Differential diagnosis:** Allergic contact dermatitis (2.3) is clinically and histologically very similar; the distinction rests on mechanism and history of sensitization rather than morphology alone.


**Image:** pic:vu021

**Priority:** HIGH-YIELD

*Source: Vulva lecture p.1, p.21*

subs.title: Allergic contact dermatitis
subs.label: COURSE
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Allergic contact dermatitis is a **type IV, T cell–mediated, delayed hypersensitivity reaction**. A foreign substance contacts the skin and links to skin proteins, forming an antigen complex that causes sensitization; on re-exposure, sensitized T cells initiate an inflammatory cascade. Common allergens include **perfumes**, additives in creams, lotions, and soaps, and chemical treatments applied to clothing.

**Clinical features:** Clinical and histologic appearance is **similar to irritant contact dermatitis**.

**Morphology (microscopic):** Features **microvesicle formation with parakeratosis**, **acanthosis**, and **spongiosis**, correlating with the clinical finding of vesicles or bullae. There is often a mixed inflammatory infiltrate with **eosinophils** and edema in the superficial dermis.

**Differential diagnosis:**

| | Irritant | Allergic |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Direct injury / cytotoxic effect | Type IV delayed hypersensitivity (requires prior sensitization) |
| Typical agents | Urine, soaps, detergents, antiseptics, deodorants | Perfumes, cream/lotion/soap additives, clothing chemicals |
| Pattern | Spongiotic | Spongiotic (microvesicles, prominent eosinophils) |

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The two forms of contact dermatitis cannot reliably be separated by morphology alone since both are spongiotic; a prominent eosinophilic infiltrate favors allergic, but the clinical history of exposure and sensitization is the real discriminator.


**Image:** pic:vu022a

**Priority:** HIGH-YIELD

*Source: Vulva lecture p.1–2, p.22*

subs.title: Lichen planus
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Lichen planus is an inflammatory **autoimmune** disease affecting skin and mucosal surfaces, including the vulva and oral mucosa.

**Clinical features:** Symptoms include **itching, burning, postcoital bleeding, dyspareunia, and pain**. On the vulva it produces well-defined **glazed erythema** of non-hair-bearing skin, with **white striae** at the periphery. Similar changes are usually seen in the **oral mucosa** of these patients; severe oral lichen planus shows a lacy, milky-white exudate overlying ulceration of the tongue.

**Morphology (microscopic):** **Hyperkeratosis**, **irregular acanthosis with elongation of the rete ridges in a saw-tooth configuration**, **focal hypergranulosis**, and **band-like (lichenoid) inflammation at the dermo-epidermal junction** — the lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate does not obscure or extend into the suprabasilar epidermis. There is **liquefactive degeneration of the basal layer** with numerous **colloid (Civatte) bodies** filling the superficial papillary dermis, with adjacent variable pigment incontinence; this correlates with dyskeratosis of the basal epidermal layer.

**Differential diagnosis:** Lichen sclerosus and lichen simplex chronicus (see comparison table in 2.6) — all three can present as white, itchy vulvar plaques, but their epidermal and dermal patterns differ sharply.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** Lichen planus is listed among the **premalignant vulvar lesions**; together with lichen sclerosus it forms the inflammatory background from which **HPV-independent (differentiated) VIN** arises (see 6.3).

**Prognosis:** Premalignant potential via the differentiated VIN pathway, in the same manner as lichen sclerosus.

subs.title: Lichen sclerosus
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Lichen sclerosus is a chronic dermatosis occurring mostly in **postmenopausal women and prepubertal girls**.

**Clinical features:** Macroscopically it produces smooth, **white plaques (leukoplakia)**, described as "porcelain white" to light pink, in the classic **figure-of-8 distribution** involving the vulva and perianal skin. The labia become **atrophic and stiffened**, with erosions and agglutination of the labia, and the **vaginal orifice becomes constricted**.

**Morphology (microscopic):** In the **early stage**, there is an **interface dermatitis** with variable degrees of epidermal hyperplasia, hyperkeratosis, and hypergranulosis, correlating clinically with a whitish plaque. In **later, established lesions**, there is prominent **dermal homogenization (hyalinization)** — a broad band of collagen deposition — together with a flattened, atrophic squamous epithelium in which the epidermis is thinned and **rete pegs disappear**. A band-like inflammatory infiltrate (activated T cells) is seen at the deeper edge of this hyalinized zone.

**Pathogenesis:** Activated T cells in a sub-epithelial inflammatory infiltrate; affected women show an increased frequency of autoimmune diseases.

**Prognosis:** Lichen sclerosus is benign; however, **1% to 5%** of women with symptomatic lichen sclerosus develop **HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma** of the vulva.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The presence of lichen sclerosus should prompt careful, **lifetime surveillance** for HPV-independent, p53-mutant VIN (see 6.3) — this progression pathway, and the associated numeric risk (1–5%), are recurrently tested facts. Do not confuse the epidermal atrophy of established lichen sclerosus with the epidermal thickening/hyperplasia seen in lichen simplex chronicus (2.6), which looks similar clinically (both cause white, itchy plaques) but is histologically almost the opposite.


**Image:** pic:vu028

**Image:** pic:vu029

**Image:** pic:vu030

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.2, p.28–30*

subs.title: Lichen simplex chronicus
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Lichen simplex chronicus is a consequence of **chronic irritation**, often caused by pruritus arising from an underlying inflammatory dermatosis (a secondary, reactive process rather than a primary disease entity).

**Clinical features:** Presents with **leukoplakia**: itchy, scaly, lichenified plaques, appearing as erythematous and excoriated papules and plaques.

**Morphology (microscopic):** **Orthokeratosis**, **hypergranulosis**, **acanthosis (epidermal hyperplasia)**, **papillary dermal fibrosis**, and **perivascular chronic inflammation**.

**Differential diagnosis / Classification (comparison table):**

| Feature | Lichen sclerosus | Lichen simplex chronicus | Lichen planus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Epidermis | Atrophic, loss of rete pegs | Acanthotic, hyperplastic | Irregular acanthosis, saw-tooth rete |
| Keratin/granular layer | Variable | Orthokeratosis, hypergranulosis | Hyperkeratosis, focal hypergranulosis |
| Dermis | Hyalinized collagen band | Papillary dermal fibrosis | Band-like infiltrate at junction |
| Inflammation | Band beneath hyalinized zone | Perivascular chronic | Lichenoid band, Civatte bodies |
| Cancer risk | 1–5% HPV-negative SCC | None if isolated | Listed as premalignant |

**Prognosis:** **No increased predisposition to cancer** when lesions are isolated — lichen simplex chronicus is explicitly **not a premalignant lesion**. This is stated as an explicit exclusion later in the clinical vulval cancer lecture as well (see 8.1).

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The single most heavily emphasized negative fact in this unit — lichen simplex chronicus, unlike lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, carries **no** increased cancer risk when it occurs in isolation. Examiners test this by listing it among a set of "premalignant vulvar lesions" and asking which one is the exception.


**Image:** pic:vu031

**Image:** pic:vu032

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.2–3, p.31–32*

subs.title: Psoriasis
subs.label: COURSE
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Psoriasis is a chronic, relapsing dermatosis characterized by a hyperproliferative epidermis.

**Clinical features:** Sharply circumscribed **erythematous psoriatic plaques and patches with overlying silvery-white scale**. On hair-bearing skin (e.g., the mons), it displays the classic **salmon-colored plaque with silvery scale**. **Inverse psoriasis**, occurring in intertriginous areas (as is typical on the vulva), shows brightly erythematous patches **without scale** — an important site-specific variation from the textbook description. At extensor sites (e.g., the knuckles, shown for comparison), the scale is described as ostraceous, silvery-white, and adherent, thick over erythematous plaques.

**Morphology (microscopic):** **Uniform (regular) psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia** with **thinning of the suprapapillary plates**; **confluent parakeratosis** and **hypogranulosis**; **intracorneal collections of neutrophils (Munro microabscesses)**; **intraspinous collections of neutrophils (spongiform pustules of Kogoj)**. Superficial perivascular lymphocytes are present, and neutrophils can be seen emigrating from the superficial dermal vessels, through the epidermis, into the zone of parakeratosis.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** **Auspitz sign** — pinpoint bleeding when the overlying scale is removed — is mechanistically linked to the histology: pulling off the scale tears away the thin suprapapillary epidermal layers, disrupting the underlying superficial blood vessels directly beneath. An examiner may ask you to explain Auspitz sign in terms of the histologic finding (thinned suprapapillary plate over dilated capillaries) rather than simply naming it. Do not confuse Munro microabscesses (stratum corneum/intracorneal) with the spongiform pustules of Kogoj (intraspinous/spinous layer) — both are neutrophilic collections but at different levels of the epidermis.

subs.title: Overview of vulvar infections
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** The major infectious causes of vulvitis named in the lecture are **HPV, HSV-1 or HSV-2, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Treponema pallidum, and Candida**. The lecture supplies a comprehensive summary table of vulvar infections with their etiologic agents, clinical manifestations, and the ancillary tests used to confirm each diagnosis.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria (Table 1 — Summary of significant vulvar infections):**

| Diagnosis | Etiologic agent | Clinical manifestation(s) | Ancillary tests |
|---|---|---|---|
| Syphilis | *Treponema pallidum* | Primary: chancre (ulcer). Secondary: condylomata lata (papule) | Dark-field examination, immunofluorescence, immunohistochemistry, PCR, serology |
| Granuloma inguinale | *Klebsiella granulomatis* | Ulcer | Culture; Warthin–Starry or Gram stain ("Donovan bodies") |
| Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) | *Chlamydia trachomatis*, types L1–L3 | Ulcer ± inguinal lymphadenopathy | Serology, culture, PCR |
| Chancroid | *Haemophilus ducreyi* | Ulcer | Culture, PCR, Gram or Giemsa stain |
| Tuberculosis | *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* | Ulcers, swellings, exophytic lesions | Culture, acid-fast stain |
| Condyloma acuminatum | HPV, usually types 6 and 11 | Condyloma acuminatum (genital warts) | Not necessary |
| Herpes | HSV types 1 and 2 | Ulcers; atypical lesions in immunosuppressed patients | Culture, PCR, immunohistochemistry |
| Varicella (vulvar shingles) | Herpes zoster | Unilateral vesicles and ulcers | PCR, immunohistochemistry |
| Molluscum contagiosum | Molluscum contagiosum virus | (genital papules) | Not necessary |
| Fungal | Various | Scaly plaques (most commonly) | Skin scrapings for KOH prep; PAS or silver stains; culture |
| Parasitic | Various | Various | Usually not necessary |

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.3, p.39–40*

subs.title: Condyloma lata vs. condyloma acuminatum, and koilocytosis
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Two lesions named "condyloma" must not be confused, since they have entirely different causes and appearances: **condylomata lata** are a manifestation of **secondary syphilis**, while **condylomata acuminata** are caused by **HPV**.

**Clinical features:** **Condylomata lata** are flat, minimally elevated lesions occurring in secondary syphilis. **Condylomata acuminata** are due to **HPV subtypes 6 and 11**; they are papillary or flat, single or multiple, and occur on the anogenital surface. They may be solitary or present as hypopigmented polypoid lesions that can become confluent, and they may become large in immunocompromised patients. Condylomata acuminata **do not commonly progress to cancer**.

**Morphology (microscopic):** Condyloma lata microscopically shows a dense, predominantly plasma cell–rich mixed inflammatory infiltrate, characteristic of secondary syphilis. Condyloma acuminatum shows, under low magnification, marked epithelial **acanthosis forming a complex papule with verrucous papillae** and areas of overlying compact ortho-/hyperkeratosis. **Koilocytes**, the hallmark of HPV cytopathic effect, are enlarged, hyperchromatic, sometimes binucleated cells with **smudgy chromatin**, often associated with clear **perinuclear halos**; viral changes may be seen only focally, in the "valleys" of the squamous epithelium.

**Differential diagnosis:** Condyloma lata (syphilis, flat, plasma cell–rich) vs. condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6/11, papillary/verrucous, koilocytes) — distinguished by clinical appearance, serology, and histology as above.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The naming trap is the single most testable point here — "lata" = syphilis, "acuminata" = HPV 6/11. Koilocytosis may be patchy/focal within the lesion, so its absence on a small superficial biopsy does not exclude HPV-related change.

*Source: Vulva lecture p.3, p.41–44*

subs.title: Herpes simplex virus vulvitis
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** A sexually transmitted disease characterized by labial ulcers with **punched-out centers**, usually caused by **HSV-2** in young women.

**Clinical features:** About **one-third** of infections are symptomatic, with lesions appearing **3–7 days after sexual contact**; lesions heal in **1–3 weeks**, but the virus remains **latent in regional nerve ganglia**. **Two-thirds** of patients suffer recurrences, which are less painful than the primary episode. There is a **high risk of transmission to the neonate during vaginal birth**, especially with an active primary infection at the time of delivery.

**Morphology (microscopic):** Infected squamous epithelium shows numerous nuclear inclusions typical of HSV: **Cowdry type A inclusions** (with a surrounding halo) and **Cowdry type B inclusions** (filling the nucleus), with an associated cluster of macrophages. **Marked ballooning** of the keratinocytes is associated with secondary **acantholysis** and **intraepidermal vesicle formation**; ballooning occurs within **24–48 hours** after infection.

**Clinical management:** Not detailed for HSV specifically in this lecture beyond the natural history above; the neonatal transmission risk is the key clinical point emphasized.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The high risk of neonatal transmission specifically during an **active primary infection** at the time of vaginal delivery is the recurrently tested obstetric point connecting this pathology topic to clinical management.

subs.title: Bartholin gland cyst
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** A Bartholin gland cyst is usually due to **vulvitis** causing **obstruction of the excretory duct** of the Bartholin gland, with resulting accumulation of gland fluid and **painful dilation**.

**Clinical features:** Bartholin gland cysts are typically located in the labia minora, near the opening of the vagina, at the **4 or 8 o'clock position**; they often appear as a smooth, domed nodule. **Primary soft tissue tumors** at this site are often mistaken for Bartholin gland cysts, because they present similarly.

**Differential diagnosis:** If infected, a Bartholin cyst may form an **abscess**; common infectious agents include **sexually transmitted organisms such as chlamydia and gonorrhea**, as well as **E. coli**. A primary soft-tissue tumor at the same anatomic site is an important clinical mimic and must be considered in a lesion that does not resolve as expected for a simple cyst.


**Image:** pic:vu048

**Image:** pic:vu049a

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.4, p.48–49*

subs.title: Other vulvovaginal cysts — Skene, Gartner, epithelial inclusion, Müllerian/mucous, canal of Nuck
subs.label: COURSE
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Beyond the Bartholin cyst, the lecture lists four further cysts under the mnemonic **BUG EM** (**B**artholin, **U**rethral/Skene, **G**artner duct, **E**pithelial inclusion, **M**üllerian/mucous), plus the canal of Nuck cyst.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria:**
- **Paraurethral (Skene) gland cyst:** rare; arises from the periurethral glands.
- **Gartner duct cyst:** rare; located in the **lateral vaginal wall**; **non-mucin-secreting**.
- **Epithelial inclusion cyst:** lined by **squamous epithelium**; may occur post-surgery or following trauma.
- **Müllerian / mucous cyst:** lined by **mucin-secreting columnar cells**.

| Cyst (BUG EM) | Site | Lining |
|---|---|---|
| Bartholin | Posterolateral introitus (4/8 o'clock) | Transitional, squamous, or mucinous |
| Urethral (Skene) | Periurethral | From periurethral glands (rare) |
| Gartner duct | Lateral vaginal wall | Low cuboidal, non-mucin-secreting |
| Epithelial inclusion | Site of prior surgery/trauma | Squamous, keratin-filled |
| Müllerian / mucous | Vestibule/vagina | Mucin-secreting columnar |

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** Location plus epithelial lining is the diagnostic key across this whole group: a non-mucinous cyst in the lateral vaginal wall is Gartner duct; a squamous-lined cyst at a surgical scar is an epithelial inclusion cyst; a mucin-secreting columnar-lined cyst is Müllerian/mucous. No lecture image is provided for these four entities (only the Bartholin cyst is illustrated).

**Priority:** HIGH-YIELD

*Source: Vulva lecture p.4*

subs.title: Anogenital mammary-like glands and hidradenoma papilliferum
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Anogenital mammary-like glands occur along the **primitive milk line**, running from the axilla to the groin; embryologically this explains the occurrence of breast-like glands and lesions on the vulva. By far the **most common lesion** arising from these anogenital mammary-like glands is **hidradenoma papilliferum**, which is also the **most common benign glandular lesion of the vulva** overall.

**Clinical features:** Hidradenoma papilliferum presents clinically as a firm, mobile, **non-ulcerated mass**, measuring less than **1 cm**. In the example given (perianal location), a coexisting hemorrhoid was noted, illustrating that this lesion can occur outside the strict vulva and be confused with other perianal/perineal masses.

**Morphology (microscopic):** The glands contain complex proliferations of **apocrine cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm** (apocrine metaplasia). The defining microscopic feature is a **dual population** of cells: **columnar cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm**, and **low cuboidal cells with clear cytoplasm** situated adjacent to the basement membrane (a myoepithelial-type outer layer beneath the secretory columnar layer).

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The dual epithelial-cell population (columnar eosinophilic + clear cuboidal) is the single most testable microscopic feature distinguishing hidradenoma papilliferum from other papillary vulvar lesions.

subs.title: Fibroepithelial (stromal) polyp
subs.label: COURSE
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** A fibroepithelial (mesodermal) stromal polyp is a benign, **hormonally related** vulvar lesion. Its stromal cells are **estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) positive**, and it occurs in **women of reproductive age**, more commonly during **pregnancy**.

**Morphology (gross):** A polypoid proliferation of the stroma with overlying squamous epithelium.

**Morphology (microscopic):** Variably cellular stroma with a **central fibrovascular core**, beneath overlying squamous epithelium.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The hormone-receptor positivity of the stromal cells and the association with pregnancy is the recurrently emphasized point distinguishing this benign, hormonally-driven polyp from other polypoid vulvar lesions.


**Image:** pic:vu055

**Image:** pic:vu056a

**Priority:** HIGH-YIELD

*Source: Vulva lecture p.4, p.55–56*

subs.title: Extramammary Paget disease
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Extramammary Paget disease is an **intraepidermal proliferation of malignant epithelial cells** in the skin of the vulva — in essence, an intraepidermal adenocarcinoma.

**Clinical features:** Clinically it presents as a **flat, scaly, eczematous, red macule or plaque**, sometimes described as moist. Because it closely mimics an inflammatory (eczematous) process, **biopsy should always be considered** in longstanding lesions that are **steroid-resistant**.

**Morphology (microscopic):** Paget cells may form variably sized **nests**, typically located at the **lower epidermis**, with preservation but compression of the basal keratinocytes. The overlying squamous epithelium often shows acanthosis and focal papillomatosis, which is not uncommon in this setting.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria:**
- **Primary Paget disease:** cutaneous origin, arising from intra-epidermal glandular cells or pluripotent cells of the epidermis or skin appendages.
- **Secondary Paget disease:** non-cutaneous origin — direct spread or metastasis from an underlying adenocarcinoma, specifically **colorectal, urothelial, ovarian, endometrial, or cervical** primary tumors.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** A diagnosis of secondary extramammary Paget disease should trigger a clinical search for an occult internal adenocarcinoma at one of the five listed primary sites. Extramammary Paget disease is explicitly listed among the vulva's premalignant lesions.


**Image:** pic:vu057

**Image:** pic:vu058

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.5, p.57–58*

subs.title: HPV-associated (usual-type) vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (uVIN)
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) is a squamous cell precursor lesion showing abnormalities of maturation, driven by either HPV infection, p53 alteration, or another mechanism. The lecture divides VIN into **HPV-associated VIN** and **HPV-independent VIN** (itself subdivided into **p53-aberrant** and **p53 wild-type** forms). Overall frequency ranking is: **HPV-associated ≫ HPV-independent, p53-mutated ≫ HPV-independent, p53 wild-type**. HPV-associated VIN typically occurs in the **4th–5th decades**, versus the **7th–8th decades** for HPV-independent VIN.

**Usual-type VIN (uVIN)** is the **precursor lesion of HPV-associated vulvar carcinoma**.

**Clinical features:** High-grade uVIN is driven by **high-risk HPV types**, most commonly **type 16**, with others including 18, 31, 33, and 45; high-grade VIN is the **most frequent type, representing more than 90%** of uVIN. A **low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion** variant is driven by low-risk HPV 6/11 as well as high-risk types. uVIN is **more common in smokers and the immunocompromised**, and is commonly seen in the **4th–5th decades**.

**Morphology (gross):** Lesions are frequently **multifocal (over 50%)**: white, erythematous, or hyperpigmented, flat or raised (papules and plaques), which may coalesce and often show irregular borders. Lesions are **acetic acid positive** on vulvoscopy.

**Morphology (microscopic):** Two patterns are recognized. The **basaloid pattern** shows small cells with a **high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio**, with basal palisading and marked cellularity. The **warty pattern** shows **epithelial thickening and papillomatosis**, with spike-like hyperkeratosis and **koilocytic change**, along with nuclear pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, mitoses, and apoptoses.

**Immunohistochemistry / molecular:** **p16 positivity in a "block" pattern** — strong, diffuse nuclear, or nuclear/cytoplasmic, staining throughout the epithelial layers.

**Prognosis:** Most low-grade VIN regress spontaneously. **Up to 9%** of high-grade VIN progress to squamous cell carcinoma **if untreated**, falling to **3–4% if treated**; spontaneous regression remains possible even after treatment, and the recurrence rate is approximately **15% after treatment**.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The basaloid pattern's small cells with peripheral palisading can, at low power, **mimic basal cell carcinoma** — a classic trap. The specific progression percentages (9% untreated, 3–4% treated, ~15% recurrence) are precise, testable numbers.

**Image:** pic:vu061

**Image:** pic:vu062

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.5–6, p.59–62*

subs.title: HPV-independent (differentiated-type) VIN — dVIN
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Differentiated-type VIN (dVIN) is **HPV-independent** and **p53-aberrant**. It is associated with the inflammatory lesions **lichen sclerosus (LS)** and **lichen planus (LP)** — the presence of lichen sclerosus should prompt careful, **lifetime surveillance** for this HPV-independent, p53-mutant VIN.

**Clinical features:** dVIN typically occurs in the **7th–8th decades**. Presentation is a long history of **itching and burning** due to the associated inflammatory process, and it is often an **incidental finding**. There is a **2–5% progression rate** from underlying lichen sclerosus or lichen planus to dVIN.

**Morphology (gross):** White patches of lichen sclerosus, associated with an irregularly raised area — an incidental raised area within a background of LS should raise suspicion for dVIN or early invasive carcinoma.

**Morphology (microscopic):** **Acanthosis**, **elongation of the rete pegs**, **basal atypia**, **parakeratosis**, and **enlarged eosinophilic cells with prominent nucleoli and intercellular bridges**. A characteristic finding is **keratin pearl formation**.

**Immunohistochemistry / molecular:** **p53 overexpression** — strongly positive, **continuous staining in the lower epithelial layers**, with an increased number of positive cells in the upper levels of the epidermis.

**Prognosis:** dVIN is **more likely to progress to invasive carcinoma (32%)** than usual-type VIN, with a **shorter latency period** to invasion. It is the recognized **precursor of verrucous carcinoma** (see 7.2).

**Classification / diagnostic criteria (the two VIN pathways compared):**

| Feature | HPV-associated VIN | HPV-independent (differentiated) VIN |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | Most common | Less common |
| Age | 4th–5th decades | 7th–8th decades |
| Background | High-risk HPV (esp. type 16); smokers, immunocompromised | Lichen sclerosus, lichen planus |
| Gross | Multifocal (>50%), acetowhite papules/plaques | White patches of LS with an irregular raised area |
| Histology | Basaloid or warty; full-thickness atypia | Basal atypia, eosinophilic cells, keratin pearls |
| Marker | p16 block-positive | p53 mutant (aberrant) pattern |
| Progression | Up to 9% untreated | 32%, shorter latency |
| Invasive outcome | HPV-associated SCC | HPV-independent SCC; verrucous carcinoma |

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** dVIN is frequently **subtle and incidental**, unlike the often obviously exophytic uVIN — a very short segment of basal atypia adjacent to lichen sclerosus is easy to under-call. The 32% progression risk (vs. up to 9% for uVIN untreated) and the shorter latency to invasion are recurrently tested, precise contrasts.

**Image:** pic:vu065

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.6, p.63–65*

subs.title: Squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva — overview and HPV-associated type
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a malignant squamous tumor associated with stromal invasion, with or without HPV association. SCC accounts for **90% of all invasive carcinomas of the vulva**, and about **5% of female genital cancers**.

**Clinical features:** **HPV-associated SCC (about 30% of cases)** occurs at **35–65 years**; **HPV-independent SCC (about 70% of cases)** occurs at **55–85 years**. **80%** of vulvar SCC arises **in the labia** (predominantly labia majora); HPV-associated tumors are often **multiple**. The **most important factor determining outcome** is **lymph node status**; the **most important factor determining lymph node metastasis** is the **depth of invasion**. Regional spread occurs to the **femoral and inguinal lymph nodes**. By frequency, vulvar malignancy histologic types rank: **squamous cell carcinoma > melanoma > basal cell carcinoma > sarcomas**.

**HPV-associated SCC** comprises the **usual/basaloid/warty types**, occurring in **premenopausal** women; it is associated with **HPV**, **smoking**, and **immunocompromise**. Etiologically it is linked to **HPV types 16 > 33 > 18**, arising on a background of HPV-associated VIN.

**Morphology (gross):** Exophytic mass or ulcerated lesion, **frequently multifocal**.

**Morphology (microscopic):** Recognized patterns include **keratinizing type**, **non-keratinizing type**, **basaloid type** (bulbous nests of cells with high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, often with peripheral palisading and associated central necrosis), and **warty type** (papillary growth that may closely simulate a condyloma acuminatum and thus be confused with it on a superficial biopsy). Generally, irregular, angulated nests infiltrate the dermis in a haphazard fashion, with central keratinization.

**Prognosis:** **5-year survival** for **FIGO stage I** is **greater than 80%**; for **FIGO stage IV** it is **10–20%**. Factors associated with recurrence include **positive or less than 3-mm margins**, tumor size, depth of invasion, and **lymphovascular and perineural invasion**.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** Warty-type SCC's papillary architecture can closely mimic a benign condyloma acuminatum on a small, superficial biopsy — a classic sampling-error trap, since misdiagnosis as benign condyloma would delay treatment of an invasive cancer.


**Image:** pic:vu067

**Image:** pic:vu068

**Image:** pic:vu069

**Image:** pic:vu070

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.7, p.67–70*

subs.title: HPV-independent SCC and verrucous carcinoma
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** HPV-independent SCC — the **differentiated/simplex type** — occurs in **postmenopausal** women, associated with background **vulvar dystrophies, especially lichen sclerosis**, and with **HPV-independent VIN**.

**Prognosis:** HPV-independent SCC has a **worse prognosis** than HPV-related SCC; **stage and lymph node involvement** are the most important prognostic factors.

**Morphology (gross):** Large, exophytic, **white mass with ulceration**.

**Morphology (microscopic):** **Keratinizing sheets** and irregularly shaped and sized **islands, cords, nests, and trabeculae**, with or without a desmoplastic stroma.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria — verrucous carcinoma:** Verrucous carcinoma is an **exo-endophytic, well-circumscribed** tumor composed of closely packed papillary structures lined by **well-differentiated stratified squamous epithelium**, with **minimal cellular atypia**. It arises as a complication of HPV-independent VIN (dVIN, see 6.3), which is its recognized precursor.

**Comparison of the two SCC pathways:**

| Feature | HPV-associated (usual/basaloid/warty) | HPV-independent (differentiated/simplex) |
|---|---|---|
| Proportion / age | ~30%; 35–65 y; premenopausal | ~70%; 55–85 y; postmenopausal |
| Risk factors | HPV 16 > 33 > 18; smoking; immunocompromise | Lichen sclerosus; HPV-independent VIN |
| Gross | Exophytic or ulcerated, often multifocal | Large white exophytic mass with ulceration |
| Histology | Basaloid, warty, (non-)keratinizing | Keratinizing; verrucous carcinoma |
| Prognosis | Better | Worse |

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** Despite arising in an older population with a background of a common benign-appearing dermatosis (lichen sclerosus), HPV-independent SCC has a **worse** prognosis than the HPV-associated form — a counter-intuitive point that is commonly tested. Verrucous carcinoma's bland cytology (minimal atypia) despite being a true invasive carcinoma is a recognized diagnostic pitfall on a superficial biopsy, analogous to the warty-SCC/condyloma trap in 7.1.


**Image:** pic:vu071

**Image:** pic:vu072

**Image:** pic:vu073

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.7–8, p.71–73*

subs.title: Other vulvar carcinomas
subs.label: SUPP
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Beyond squamous cell carcinoma, the lecture lists several other epithelial malignancies of the vulva: **basal cell carcinoma (BCC)**, **endometrioid carcinoma**, and **Bartholin gland carcinoma**, which may take the form of an **adenocarcinoma** or an **adenoid cystic carcinoma**.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria:** By overall frequency of histologic type, vulvar malignancy ranks: **squamous cell carcinoma > melanoma > basal cell carcinoma > sarcomas** (repeated from 7.1 for completeness at this point in the lecture).

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** Melanoma, not basal cell carcinoma, is the **second most common** vulvar malignancy by histologic type — an easy point to get backwards.

No image in the lecture's inventory corresponds to this specific sub-topic (BCC, endometrioid, or Bartholin gland carcinoma are not separately illustrated).

**Priority:** SUPPORTING

*Source: Vulva lecture p.9*

subs.title: Mesenchymal neoplasms of the vulva
subs.label: SUPP
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Three characteristic mesenchymal (soft tissue) tumors of the vulva are described, distinguished largely by their cellularity and vascular pattern at low power.

**Morphology (gross):** **Cellular angiofibroma** characteristically presents as a small, nodular, subcutaneous mass with a firm or rubbery consistency; it typically has a **well-circumscribed** border, though occasionally there may be focal infiltration of surrounding tissue.

**Morphology (microscopic):**
- **Cellular angiofibroma:** well-circumscribed, cellular lesion with numerous vessels.
- **Angiomyofibroblastoma:** on low-power examination, characterized by numerous **capillary-sized vessels** and **alternating zones of cellularity**. In women, it typically arises in the subcutaneous tissue of the vulva, but the same entity can occur in men, in the scrotum or paratesticular soft tissue.
- **Aggressive (deep) angiomyxoma:** on low-power examination, a uniformly **paucicellular** neoplasm containing evenly dispersed **medium- to large-sized vessels**.

| Tumor | Key low-power features |
|---|---|
| Cellular angiofibroma | Well-circumscribed, cellular, many vessels; firm/rubbery subcutaneous nodule |
| Angiomyofibroblastoma | Capillary-sized vessels; alternating cellular zones |
| Aggressive angiomyxoma | Uniformly paucicellular; medium–large vessels evenly dispersed |

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** These three vascular/myofibroblastic vulvar mesenchymal tumors are frequently confused with one another; the discriminating feature in each case is the **cellularity pattern and vessel caliber**: angiofibroma = cellular + well-circumscribed; angiomyofibroblastoma = alternating cellular zones + capillary-sized vessels; angiomyxoma = paucicellular + medium-to-large vessels.

**Image:** pic:vu075

**Image:** pic:vu076

**Priority:** SUPPORTING

*Source: Vulva lecture p.9, p.74–76*

lectures.title: Clinical: Diagnosis, Staging & Treatment of Vulvar Cancer

sections.title: Clinical: Vulval Cancer (Presentation, Diagnosis, Spread, Staging)

subs.title: Epidemiology, premalignant lesions, and clinical features
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Vulval cancer has a **peak age of incidence of 65–75 years**, associated with vulvar dystrophies in older women; in **younger women** it is associated with **HPV infection**.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria — premalignant vulvar lesions:** **Lichen sclerosis; lichen planus; Paget's disease of the vulva; vulval intraepithelial neoplasia.** **Note: lichen simplex chronicus is explicitly NOT a premalignant lesion** — this exclusion is stated directly in the source material as a named exception to the list, reinforcing the point already made in 2.6.

**Clinical features:** The **most common symptom is pruritus**. On examination, findings may include a **hypopigmented area**, a **macule/papule**, a **warty growth**, or **hyperpigmented areas**. Diagnosis is made on **biopsy**. Histologic types by frequency: **squamous cell cancer > melanoma > basal cell cancer > sarcomas** (as in 7.1/7.3). Vulvar SCC subtypes recapitulate the two pathways already described: the **usual/basaloid/warty type** occurs in **premenopausal** women, is associated with **HPV** (most commonly HPV **16 and 33**) and with **smoking and immunocompromise**; the **differentiated/simplex type** occurs in **post-menopausal** women, associated with background vulvar dystrophies, especially **lichen sclerosis**.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The explicit exclusion of lichen simplex chronicus from the premalignant list is one of the most reliably testable single facts in the entire vulva syllabus — it appears as a standalone "Note" in the original lecture, signaling deliberate emphasis by the lecturer.


**Image:** pic:vu077a

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.77*

subs.title: Diagnostic biopsy technique
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** Diagnosis of vulval cancer is made on **biopsy**. If an area needs to be identified for biopsy, **vulvoscopy** can be used.

**Clinical management (diagnostic procedure):** Vulvoscopy technique: apply **5% acetic acid** and **wait 5 minutes** for an abnormal white area to appear, or alternatively use **1% toluidine blue**. A **special biopsy forceps — the Keyes biopsy forceps** — is used (if unavailable, a knife biopsy is performed instead). A **deeper chunk of tissue** should be biopsied: to **rule out invasion**, the biopsy should include the **full thickness of the epidermis and some part of the dermis**.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** A superficial biopsy that fails to include dermis cannot rule out stromal invasion, which is the entire point of adequate depth — this connects directly to the FIGO IA/IB distinction in 8.3, which hinges on measured depth of stromal invasion.

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.77*

subs.title: Lymphatic drainage and FIGO staging
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Definition/overview:** The **most common location** of vulval cancer is the **labia (labia majora)**. The **most common route of spread** is **lymphatics > direct > hematogenous**.

**Clinical features (lymphatic drainage):** Lymphatic spread proceeds from the **superficial inguinal lymph nodes**, down to the **deep inguinal lymph nodes** (located in the femoral canal) — the most superior of which are **Cloquet's lymph nodes** (also called the lymph nodes of Rosenmüller) — and then onward to the **pelvic lymph nodes**. Some lymphatics from the **clitoris** can drain **directly into the deep inguinal lymph nodes**. **Midline areas** (e.g., clitoris, anterior labia minora, fourchette) drain **bilaterally**; the **lateral area of the vulva** drains **predominantly to the ipsilateral group** of lymph nodes. The **most important prognostic factor is lymphatic spread**. These inguinofemoral lymph nodes are clinically palpable and can be examined directly.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria — FIGO staging:**

| Stage | Definition |
|---|---|
| I | Limited to the vulva |
| IA | ≤2 cm size and ≤1 mm stromal invasion (microinvasive carcinoma) |
| IB | >2 cm size or >1 mm stromal invasion |
| II | Extension to the lower 1/3 of the vagina, urethra, or anus |
| III | Inguinofemoral lymph nodes positive |
| IVA | Fixed and ulcerated inguinofemoral lymph nodes; or extension to the upper 2/3 of the vagina and urethra |
| IVB | Distant metastases and pelvic lymph nodes |

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** Pelvic lymph node involvement is staged as **IVB**, not stage III — a very commonly tested trap, since stage III is defined only by *inguinofemoral* (not pelvic) nodal disease. The IA/IB cutoffs (≤2 cm AND ≤1 mm invasion for IA; either criterion exceeded moves to IB) must be applied as a combined size-and-depth rule, not either criterion alone.

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.77*

---

subs.title: Surgical management by stage and inguinofemoral lymph node dissection (IFLND)
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Clinical management:** For **Stage IA** disease (≤2 cm size and ≤1 mm invasion), treatment is **wide local excision**, with **at least a 2 cm tumor-free margin**. For **Stage IB** disease (>2 cm size or >1 mm invasion), treatment is **radical excision**, with **at least a 3–4 cm tumor-free margin**. With larger tumors, this may escalate to a **radical total vulvectomy or hemivulvectomy**. For **Stage II** disease (lower 1/3 of vagina, urethra, or anus involved), treatment is **radical total vulvectomy**.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria — IFLND decision rule for early vulvar cancers:**

| Stage Ia and no LVSI | Stage Ia + LVSI, or Ib/II |
|---|---|
| No lymph node dissection required | IFLND required |

If the lesion is **lateral**: an **ipsilateral IFLND** is performed; if the frozen section is positive, a **contralateral IFLND** is then also performed. If the lesion is **midline/central** (within **1 cm of the midline** — e.g., clitoris, anterior labia, fourchette), a **bilateral IFLND** is performed.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The decision to proceed to contralateral IFLND for a lateral lesion depends specifically on the **frozen-section result of the ipsilateral nodes** — a stepwise, intraoperative decision rule rather than a fixed plan decided before surgery. Whether a lesion counts as "midline" for bilateral IFLND purposes is defined precisely as **within 1 cm of the midline**.


**Image:** pic:vu079

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.78–79*

subs.title: Adjuvant radiotherapy and sentinel lymph node sampling
subs.label: COURSE + EXAM
subs.md:
**Clinical management:** Post-operative **pelvic radiotherapy** is required if any of the following are present: **≥2 lymph nodes positive** for tumor; **extracapsular spread**, even in just 1 lymph node; or a **disease-free margin of less than 8 mm**. For **advanced stage IVA**, treatment is **chemoradiation**. (Stage IVB management is not further detailed beyond the general principle that it represents disseminated disease.)

**Sentinel lymph node sampling:** The purpose of sentinel lymph node sampling is to **avoid** the morbidity of a full lymph node dissection. Problems associated with extensive/full IFLND include **lymphedema** (swollen lower limbs) and risk of **wound dehiscence**. The **sentinel lymph node** is defined as the **first lymph node draining the area of concern**; it is identified by injecting **isosulfan blue** or **radiolabelled technetium**. Eligibility for sentinel node sampling (rather than full IFLND) requires a **unifocal tumor, less than 4 cm**, with **no clinically suspicious lymph nodes**.

**Classification / diagnostic criteria — sentinel node frozen section decision:**

| If sentinel node +ve on frozen section | If sentinel node −ve on frozen section |
|---|---|
| Proceed with full IFLND | Omit further dissection |

If the sentinel node is positive for tumor, the rest of the nodes could be involved; if the sentinel node is negative, the rest of the nodes are **presumed negative** as well, and further dissection is omitted.

**Diagnostic pitfalls / exam traps:** The three specific triggers for adjuvant pelvic radiotherapy (≥2 positive nodes; any extracapsular spread; margin <8 mm) are exact, testable numeric criteria, not a vague "if nodes are involved" rule. The eligibility criteria for sentinel node sampling (unifocal, <4 cm, clinically negative nodes) must all be satisfied together.

**Priority:** MUST-KNOW

*Source: Vulva lecture p.78–79*
