stem: The vestibule ('inner vulva') is defined as the region extending between which two anatomic landmarks?
options: The mons pubis and the perineum
The labia majora and the labia minora
questions.explanation: The vestibule extends from Hart's line (the mucocutaneous junction on the medial labia minora) to the hymen; four structures open into it: the Bartholin glands, minor vestibular glands, Skene glands, and the urethra.
questions.objective: Define the anatomic boundaries of the vulvar vestibule

stem: The ducts of the major vestibular (Bartholin) glands open into the vestibule, posterolateral to the hymen, at which clock positions?
questions.explanation: The Bartholin ducts enter the vestibule posterolaterally adjacent to the hymen, corresponding to the 4 and 8 o'clock positions clinically — the classic site of a Bartholin cyst or abscess.
questions.objective: Localise the clinical opening site of the Bartholin ducts

stem: A vulvar skin biopsy (image shown) shows keratinized squamous epithelium overlying dermis that contains collagen, adipose tissue, and sebaceous glands with associated hair follicles.
These findings are most consistent with tissue obtained from which site?
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue and adnexal (pilosebaceous) structures are typical of the labia majora and are absent in the labia minora/vestibule; this is a useful microscopic clue to site of origin.
questions.objective: Use dermal/adnexal composition to localise a vulvar biopsy

stem: A 53-year-old postmenopausal woman has pale, parchment-like areas involving the labia majora, labia minora and introitus, with a narrowed introitus.
A biopsy shows thinning of the squamous epithelium, a dense band of upper dermal hyaline collagen and scattered mononuclear cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Epidermal atrophy with loss of rete pegs and a broad band of homogenised (hyalinized) dermal collagen is diagnostic of established lichen sclerosus; 1-5% of symptomatic women develop HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma, so lifetime surveillance is required.
questions.objective: Recognise the histology of lichen sclerosus and its malignant potential

stem: A 40-year-old woman has had pruritic patches on her vulva for 4 months. Examination shows multiple 1.5-3 cm white, scaly plaques. Biopsy of one lesion shows hyperorthokeratosis, hypergranulosis, irregular acanthosis, and papillary dermal fibrosis; keratinocyte mitoses are present but without atypia.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Orthokeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis and papillary dermal fibrosis without cytologic atypia are the defining features of lichen simplex chronicus (historically termed 'squamous cell hyperplasia'); unlike lichen sclerosus/planus it carries no increased cancer risk when isolated.
questions.objective: Distinguish lichen simplex chronicus from its clinical mimics by histology

stem: Vulvar inflammatory dermatoses are organized by histologic reaction pattern. Which of the following is classified under the ACANTHOTIC reaction pattern?
questions.explanation: The acanthotic pattern (formerly 'squamous cell hyperplasia') includes psoriasis and lichen simplex chronicus. Lichen sclerosus is lichenoid/dermal-homogenization, pemphigoid is vesiculobullous, and Behçet disease is vasculopathic.
questions.objective: Classify vulvar dermatoses by histologic reaction pattern

stem: A 34-year-old woman develops well-defined erythematous vulvar papules and plaques shortly after switching to a new antiseptic soap, with no prior history of sensitization to the product.
Which mechanism best explains this presentation?
questions.explanation: Irritant contact dermatitis results from direct skin injury or cytotoxic effects of substances such as soaps, detergents, antiseptics and urine — it is not immune-mediated and does not require prior sensitization, unlike allergic contact dermatitis (type IV hypersensitivity).
questions.objective: Differentiate irritant from allergic contact dermatitis by mechanism

stem: A 28-year-old woman develops pruritic vulvar vesicles after using a new perfumed soap. Biopsy shows microvesicle formation with parakeratosis, acanthosis, spongiosis, and a mixed dermal infiltrate rich in eosinophils.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Microvesicles with parakeratosis, acanthosis, spongiosis and a prominent eosinophilic infiltrate correlate with the clinical vesicles/bullae of allergic (type IV hypersensitivity) contact dermatitis; a prominent eosinophilic infiltrate favors allergic over irritant contact dermatitis.
questions.objective: Recognise the histology of allergic contact dermatitis

stem: A 45-year-old woman has well-defined glazed erythema of the vulva with white striae at the periphery, plus similar changes in the oral mucosa. Biopsy (image shown) shows irregular acanthosis with elongated, saw-tooth rete ridges, a dense band-like lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction, and colloid (Civatte) bodies.
Which finding is most characteristic of this entity, as distinct from lichen sclerosus?
options: Saw-tooth rete ridge elongation with Civatte bodies
Loss of rete pegs with epidermal atrophy
questions.explanation: Lichen planus shows irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges, a band-like lichenoid infiltrate, and colloid (Civatte) bodies from basal layer liquefactive degeneration — the opposite pattern to lichen sclerosus, which shows epidermal atrophy and dermal hyalinization.
questions.objective: Identify the characteristic microscopic features of lichen planus

stem: A 36-year-old sexually active woman reports warty vulvar lesions increasing in size and number over 5 years. Examination shows multiple 0.5-2 cm, red-pink, flattened lesions with rough surfaces on the vulva and perineum. Biopsy of a larger lesion shows marked acanthosis with verrucous papillae and koilocytic change.
Which of the following infectious agents is most likely to produce these lesions?
questions.explanation: Condylomata acuminata are caused by HPV, usually low-risk types 6 and 11, producing papillary/verrucous acanthosis with koilocytic change; they do not commonly progress to cancer. Condylomata lata (flat, syphilitic) and other infections in the summary table are distractors here.
questions.objective: Identify HPV as the cause of vulvar condylomata

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with dysuria, vulvar pain and itching, fever and fatigue for several days. She has a new sexual partner. Examination shows inguinal lymphadenopathy and tender vesicular lesions covering both labia majora and the perineum.
This patient's infection can lead to which of the following?
questions.explanation: HSV establishes latency in regional nerve ganglia; about two-thirds of patients suffer recurrences (which are less painful than the primary episode). Locomotor ataxia (tabes dorsalis) is a late manifestation of syphilis, not HSV, and HSV is not a recognised cause of vulvar SCC.
questions.objective: Recognise the natural history and recurrence of HSV vulvitis

stem: A patient with secondary syphilis develops flat, minimally elevated anogenital papules.
These flat lesions of secondary syphilis are correctly termed:
questions.explanation: 'Condylomata lata' are a manifestation of secondary syphilis (Treponema pallidum), flat and plasma-cell rich, and must not be confused with 'condylomata acuminata', the HPV 6/11-driven papillary/verrucous warts.
questions.objective: Distinguish condyloma lata from condyloma acuminatum by cause

stem: A biopsy of a vulvar papule (image shown) shows enlarged, sometimes binucleated squamous cells with hyperchromatic, smudgy chromatin and clear perinuclear halos, seen focally in the 'valleys' of a papillary, acanthotic epithelium.
This cytopathic finding is characteristic of infection with which agent?
questions.explanation: Koilocytes — enlarged cells with smudgy chromatin and perinuclear halos — are the hallmark cytopathic effect of HPV infection; viral change may be patchy, so its absence on a small biopsy does not exclude HPV.
questions.objective: Recognise koilocytosis as the cytopathic hallmark of HPV infection

stem: A 25-year-old woman has had dyspareunia for one month. Examination shows a tender, focal swelling on the left posterolateral inner labium, with no external genital lesions otherwise. A 3-cm cystic lesion filled with purulent exudate is excised.
In which of the following structures did this lesion most likely develop?
questions.explanation: The Bartholin ducts enter the vestibule posterolaterally adjacent to the hymen (4/8 o'clock); obstruction of the duct with secondary infection produces a painful cystic/abscess lesion at this exact site.
questions.objective: Localize Bartholin gland cysts/abscesses anatomically

stem: A gross specimen (image shown) shows a smooth, domed cystic nodule arising from obstruction of a major vestibular gland duct.
Where does this type of cyst most characteristically form?
options: 3 and 9 o'clock positions at the urethral meatus
4 and 8 o'clock positions near the hymen
questions.explanation: A Bartholin duct cyst results from vulvitis-related obstruction of the excretory duct, classically located in the labia minora near the vaginal opening at the 4 or 8 o'clock position, presenting as a smooth domed nodule.
questions.objective: Localise the Bartholin duct cyst clinically and on gross pathology

stem: A cystic lesion is found in the lateral vaginal wall, lined by low cuboidal, non-mucin-secreting epithelium.
This is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: Gartner duct cysts are rare, located specifically in the lateral vaginal wall, and are non-mucin-secreting — distinguishing them from the mucin-secreting Müllerian cyst and from Bartholin and epithelial inclusion cysts.
questions.objective: Identify Gartner duct cyst by site and epithelial lining

stem: A firm, mobile, non-ulcerated vulvar nodule less than 1 cm is excised. Microscopy (image shown) shows a complex papillary proliferation with a dual population of cells.
The dual cell population characteristic of this lesion consists of:
options: Columnar apocrine cells (eosinophilic cytoplasm) and clear low-cuboidal myoepithelial-type cells
Sebaceous cells with associated hair follicles
questions.explanation: Hidradenoma papilliferum, the most common benign glandular lesion of the vulva, shows a characteristic dual population: columnar cells with abundant eosinophilic (apocrine) cytoplasm, and low cuboidal clear cells adjacent to the basement membrane.
questions.objective: Recognise the dual cell population of hidradenoma papilliferum

stem: Vulvar hidradenoma papilliferum arises from anogenital mammary-like glands located along which embryologic structure?
questions.explanation: Anogenital mammary-like glands occur along the primitive milk line (running from axilla to groin), which embryologically explains the occurrence of breast-like glands and lesions (e.g., fibroadenoma, hidradenoma papilliferum) on the vulva.
questions.objective: Explain the embryologic origin of vulvar breast-like glandular lesions

stem: A 29-year-old pregnant woman develops a polypoid vulvar lesion. Immunohistochemistry shows the stromal cells are estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor positive.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Fibroepithelial (mesodermal) stromal polyps are benign, hormonally-related lesions whose stromal cells are ER/PR positive, occurring in women of reproductive age, more commonly during pregnancy.
questions.objective: Recognise the clinical association of the fibroepithelial stromal polyp

stem: A 57-year-old woman has a 0.7-cm flat, white area on the right labia majora. Biopsy shows dysplastic cells occupying almost the full thickness of the squamous epithelium with minimal underlying chronic inflammation. In-situ hybridization demonstrates HPV type 16 DNA in the epithelial cells.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Full-thickness squamous dysplasia with demonstrated high-risk HPV16 is diagnostic of usual-type (HPV-associated) VIN, the precursor lesion of HPV-associated vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.
questions.objective: Diagnose usual-type VIN from HPV in-situ hybridization and full-thickness dysplasia

stem: A 52-year-old woman has a red, pruritic, rough, scaly lesion on the left labium, 0.4 x 0.9 cm, increasing in size over 7 months. No lymphadenopathy or rectal lesions are found, and the Pap smear is normal. Biopsy shows large atypical cells lying singly or in small clusters within the epidermis, with abundant PAS-positive cytoplasm.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Large PAS-positive Paget cells scattered singly or in nests within the epidermis are diagnostic of extramammary Paget disease, an intraepidermal adenocarcinoma; a search for an underlying/associated adenocarcinoma (colorectal, urothelial, ovarian, endometrial, cervical) should follow if secondary disease is suspected.
questions.objective: Recognise the cytology of extramammary Paget disease

stem: Human papillomavirus is involved in the pathogenesis of all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
questions.explanation: Differentiated (dVIN) is the HPV-independent, p53-aberrant VIN subtype, arising on a background of lichen sclerosus/lichen planus rather than HPV infection. Condyloma, warty (usual-type) VIN, and cervical SCC are all HPV-driven.
questions.objective: Identify which VIN subtype is HPV-independent

stem: An elderly woman with extramammary Paget disease of the vulva is found on further work-up to have an underlying colorectal adenocarcinoma.
This presentation represents which type of extramammary Paget disease?
questions.explanation: Secondary Paget disease is of non-cutaneous origin, representing direct spread or metastasis from an underlying adenocarcinoma (colorectal, urothelial, ovarian, endometrial, or cervical), and should trigger a search for an occult internal primary.
questions.objective: Distinguish primary from secondary extramammary Paget disease

stem: On histology of extramammary Paget disease, Paget cells characteristically form nests located predominantly at which level of the epidermis?
options: Lower epidermis, with compression of the basal keratinocytes
questions.explanation: Paget cells form variably sized nests typically at the lower epidermis, with preservation but compression of the basal keratinocytes; the overlying epithelium often shows acanthosis and focal papillomatosis.
questions.objective: Localise Paget cells within the epidermis

stem: A patient has multifocal white/erythematous, acetowhite vulvar plaques. Biopsy (image shown) shows small basaloid cells with a high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, marked cellularity, and peripheral palisading.
This basaloid pattern of high-grade usual-type VIN can be mistaken, at low power, for which entity?
questions.explanation: The basaloid pattern of usual-type VIN — small cells with high N:C ratio and peripheral palisading — is a classic low-power mimic of basal cell carcinoma, a recognised diagnostic trap.
questions.objective: Recognise the basal cell carcinoma mimicry of basaloid VIN

stem: A 48-year-old woman has a multifocal, exophytic vulvar mass, HPV16-positive. Biopsy (image shown) shows bulbous nests of cells with high N:C ratio, peripheral palisading, and central necrosis.
This basaloid pattern of squamous cell carcinoma is most closely associated with which risk factor?
questions.explanation: The basaloid pattern is one of the HPV-associated (usual/basaloid/warty) SCC subtypes, etiologically linked to HPV types 16 > 33 > 18, arising on a background of HPV-associated VIN in predominantly premenopausal women.
questions.objective: Identify the basaloid pattern of HPV-associated vulvar SCC

stem: A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman with a long history of lichen sclerosus develops a keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva.
This HPV-independent (differentiated/simplex) SCC subtype is most strongly associated with which background condition?
questions.explanation: HPV-independent (differentiated/simplex) SCC occurs in postmenopausal women and is associated with background vulvar dystrophies, especially lichen sclerosis, and with HPV-independent VIN — in contrast to the HPV/smoking/immunocompromise risk profile of HPV-associated SCC.
questions.objective: Associate HPV-independent SCC with vulvar dystrophies

stem: Which statement correctly compares the two pathways of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma?
options: HPV-independent SCC has a better prognosis despite occurring in older patients
HPV-associated SCC has a worse prognosis overall
HPV-independent SCC has a worse prognosis than HPV-associated SCC
Prognosis does not differ between the two pathways
questions.explanation: Despite arising in an older population against a background of the common, benign-appearing lichen sclerosus, HPV-independent SCC has a worse prognosis than HPV-associated SCC — a counter-intuitive, frequently tested point.
questions.objective: Compare prognosis between HPV-associated and HPV-independent SCC

stem: An elderly woman has a large, exo-endophytic, well-circumscribed vulvar mass. Biopsy shows closely packed papillary structures lined by well-differentiated stratified squamous epithelium with minimal cellular atypia.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Verrucous carcinoma is exo-endophytic and well-circumscribed, with well-differentiated squamous epithelium and minimal cytologic atypia despite being a true invasive carcinoma — a recognised pitfall on superficial biopsy, analogous to the warty-SCC/condyloma trap.
questions.objective: Recognise verrucous carcinoma and its bland cytology despite malignancy

stem: Verrucous carcinoma of the vulva is recognized as arising as a complication of which precursor lesion?
questions.explanation: Verrucous carcinoma arises as a complication of HPV-independent (differentiated) VIN, which is its recognised precursor lesion.
questions.objective: Identify the precursor lesion of verrucous carcinoma

stem: Ranked by overall frequency, which sequence of vulvar malignancy histologic types is correct?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma > basal cell carcinoma > melanoma > sarcoma
Squamous cell carcinoma > melanoma > basal cell carcinoma > sarcoma
Melanoma > squamous cell carcinoma > basal cell carcinoma > sarcoma
Squamous cell carcinoma > sarcoma > melanoma > basal cell carcinoma
questions.explanation: By frequency, vulvar malignancy histologic types rank squamous cell carcinoma (90% of invasive vulvar carcinomas) > melanoma > basal cell carcinoma > sarcomas.
questions.objective: Rank vulvar malignancy subtypes by frequency

stem: A 64-year-old woman, postmenopausal with a 30-year smoking history, has a 1-cm nonfriable white plaque on the right labia majora that has slowly enlarged over a year. Biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma. A sentinel lymph node biopsy is planned for staging.
This procedure should target which of the following lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: Vulvar carcinoma spreads first to the superficial and then deep inguinofemoral lymph nodes before reaching the pelvic nodes; lymph node status is the single most important prognostic factor, so these are the nodes targeted for sentinel sampling.
questions.objective: Identify the primary regional nodal basin for vulvar SCC

stem: Vulval cancer has a peak age of incidence of:
questions.explanation: Vulval cancer has a peak age of incidence of 65-75 years, associated with vulvar dystrophies in older women; in younger women it is associated with HPV infection.
questions.objective: Quote the peak age of incidence of vulval cancer

stem: Which of the following is explicitly NOT considered a premalignant lesion of the vulva?
questions.explanation: The premalignant vulvar lesions are lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, Paget disease, and VIN. Lichen simplex chronicus is explicitly stated as NOT premalignant, carrying no increased cancer risk when isolated — one of the most reliably tested single facts in this topic.
questions.objective: Identify the lesion explicitly excluded from the premalignant list

stem: When performing a vulvar biopsy to evaluate a suspicious lesion, which principle is essential to reliably exclude stromal invasion?
options: Use only a superficial shave biopsy
Avoid sampling the dermis to minimize bleeding
Sample only the center of any ulcerated area
Obtain the full thickness of the epidermis with some underlying dermis
questions.explanation: A superficial biopsy that fails to include dermis cannot rule out stromal invasion; the biopsy should include the full thickness of the epidermis and some part of the dermis, which is essential for applying the FIGO IA/IB depth-of-invasion criteria.
questions.objective: Explain why biopsy depth matters for excluding invasion

stem: During vulvoscopy, after application of 5% acetic acid, how long should one wait before an abnormal white area becomes apparent?
questions.explanation: Vulvoscopy technique involves applying 5% acetic acid and waiting 5 minutes for an abnormal white (acetowhite) area to appear, or alternatively using 1% toluidine blue; a Keyes biopsy forceps is then used to sample the identified area.
questions.objective: Recall the acetic acid application time in vulvoscopy

stem: Surgical management of FIGO stage IA vulvar carcinoma (≤2 cm size, ≤1 mm invasion) consists of wide local excision with a minimum tumor-free margin of:
questions.explanation: Stage IA disease is treated with wide local excision with at least a 2 cm tumor-free margin; larger, deeper-invading stage IB disease requires radical excision with a 3-4 cm margin.
questions.objective: Recall the required margin for wide local excision in stage IA disease

stem: For FIGO stage IB vulvar carcinoma (>2 cm size or >1 mm invasion), radical excision requires a minimum tumor-free margin of:
questions.explanation: Stage IB disease requires radical excision with at least a 3-4 cm tumor-free margin; with larger tumors this may escalate to radical total vulvectomy or hemivulvectomy.
questions.objective: Recall the required margin for radical excision in stage IB disease

stem: A patient has FIGO stage IA vulvar squamous cell carcinoma without lymphovascular space invasion (LVSI) (surgical diagram shown).
What is the appropriate management regarding inguinofemoral lymph node dissection (IFLND)?
options: No lymph node dissection is required
questions.explanation: For stage IA disease without LVSI, no lymph node dissection is required; IFLND is required for stage Ia with LVSI, or for stage Ib/II disease.
questions.objective: Apply the IFLND decision rule for stage IA disease without LVSI

stem: In a patient with a lateral vulvar carcinoma undergoing ipsilateral IFLND, a positive frozen section of the ipsilateral nodes should prompt:
options: Repeat biopsy of the primary tumor
questions.explanation: For a lateral lesion, an ipsilateral IFLND is performed first; if the frozen section is positive, a contralateral IFLND is then also performed — a stepwise, intraoperative decision rather than a fixed pre-operative plan.
questions.objective: Apply the stepwise, frozen-section-driven IFLND decision rule for lateral lesions

checks.q: The vestibule of the vulva extends from which landmark to which landmark?
checks.expl: The vestibule is the 'inner vulva,' extending from Hart's line (the mucocutaneous junction) to the hymen.

checks.q: The Bartholin ducts enter the vestibule posterolaterally, adjacent to the hymen, corresponding to the [ blank ] and [ blank ] o'clock positions.
checks.expl: This is the classic site where a Bartholin cyst or abscess presents.

checks.q: Compared with the normal cervix, perinuclear vacuoles (koilocyte-like clearing) found in vulvar squamous epithelium should be interpreted as:
options: A normal glycogenation finding, as in the cervix
A normal feature of the basal layer
checks.expl: Cytoplasmic glycogen and its vacuoles are largely absent from normal vulvar epithelium; their presence is abnormal and HPV-related, unlike in the cervix.

checks.q: The labia majora are lined by [ blank ] stratified squamous epithelium, while the vestibule and labia minora are lined by [ blank ] squamous epithelium.
checks.expl: This is the key site-based distinction in normal vulvar epithelial histology.

checks.q: In normal vulvar epithelium, the basal cell layer has a higher nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio than more superficial layers.
checks.expl: Cells mature gradually toward the surface, with the basal layer showing the highest N:C ratio.

checks.q: A vulvar biopsy showing adipose tissue and pilosebaceous (adnexal) structures most favors origin from:
checks.expl: Adnexal structures and adipose tissue are typically absent in the labia minora, making their presence a useful clue to labia majora origin.

checks.q: Adnexal structures and adipose tissue are typically absent in the labia minora.
checks.expl: This absence is a recognized histologic discriminator between labia majora and labia minora.

checks.q: Match each component of the Bartholin gland/duct complex with its characteristic histology.
right: Small, bland, pyknotic nuclei with abundant pale blue-grey cytoplasm in densely collagenized stroma
checks.expl: Each of the three components has a distinct, site-specific epithelial lining.

checks.q: The urothelial-type (transitional) epithelium of the main Bartholin duct should be interpreted as evidence of a urothelial contaminant rather than a normal finding.
checks.expl: This transitional epithelium is a normal finding at this specific site, not a contaminant or a sign of a different process.

checks.q: Match each histologic reaction pattern with an example vulvar dermatosis.
checks.expl: Vulvar inflammatory dermatoses are organized by the histologic reaction pattern they produce.

checks.q: Lichen sclerosus appears in only a single reaction-pattern row of the classification.
checks.expl: Lichen sclerosus appears in two rows — lichenoid (early) and dermal homogenization/sclerosis (established) — reflecting its evolution over time.

checks.q: "Squamous cell hyperplasia" is the older, historical name for which reaction pattern?
checks.expl: The acanthotic pattern was formerly termed squamous cell hyperplasia.

checks.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a typical irritant causing irritant contact dermatitis of the vulva?
checks.expl: Perfume is a typical allergen causing allergic contact dermatitis (2.3), not a listed irritant for the irritant form.

checks.q: Irritant contact dermatitis is immune-mediated.
checks.expl: It results from direct skin injury, cytotoxic effect, or inflammation from contact with an irritant — it is not immune-mediated, unlike allergic contact dermatitis.

checks.q: Which microscopic features are described for allergic contact dermatitis? (Select all that apply.)
options: Eosinophils in a mixed inflammatory infiltrate
checks.expl: Allergic contact dermatitis shows microvesicles with parakeratosis, acanthosis, spongiosis, and a mixed infiltrate with eosinophils; granulomas are not a feature.

checks.q: Allergic contact dermatitis is mediated by which hypersensitivity reaction?
checks.expl: It is a type IV, T cell-mediated, delayed hypersensitivity reaction requiring prior sensitization.

checks.q: Which histologic feature is characteristic of lichen planus?
options: Irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges and a band-like lichenoid infiltrate
Dermal hyalinization with loss of rete pegs
checks.expl: Lichen planus shows irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges, hyperkeratosis, and a band-like lichenoid infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction.

checks.q: Lichen planus shows [ blank ] degeneration of the basal layer with numerous [ blank ] bodies filling the superficial papillary dermis.
checks.expl: Liquefactive degeneration of the basal layer with colloid (Civatte) bodies is characteristic of lichen planus.

checks.q: Lichen planus is listed among the premalignant vulvar lesions, forming part of the differentiated VIN pathway together with lichen sclerosus.
checks.expl: Lichen planus and lichen sclerosus together form the inflammatory background from which HPV-independent (differentiated) VIN arises.

checks.q: Between 1% and 5% of women with symptomatic lichen sclerosus develop HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva.
checks.expl: This 1-5% progression risk is an explicitly stated, recurrently tested numeric fact.

checks.q: The classic gross distribution of lichen sclerosus is described as:
options: A figure-of-8 pattern involving the vulva and perianal skin
A linear distribution along Hart's line
A circumferential ring around the urethra
checks.expl: Lichen sclerosus classically presents as porcelain-white plaques in a figure-of-8 distribution over the vulva and perianal skin.

checks.q: Which features characterize established (late-stage) lichen sclerosus on microscopy? (Select all that apply.)
options: Band-like infiltrate at the deep edge of the hyalinized zone
checks.expl: Acanthosis/epidermal hyperplasia is a feature of early lichen sclerosus (and of lichen simplex chronicus), not established, late-stage lichen sclerosus, which is atrophic.

checks.q: Which condition can mimic lichen sclerosus clinically (both cause white, itchy plaques) but shows epidermal thickening rather than epidermal atrophy?
checks.expl: Lichen simplex chronicus is histologically almost the opposite of established lichen sclerosus despite a similar clinical appearance.

checks.q: Lichen simplex chronicus, when occurring in isolation, carries no increased predisposition to cancer.
checks.expl: This is the single most heavily emphasized negative fact in this unit — lichen simplex chronicus is explicitly not premalignant when isolated.

checks.q: Match each histologic description to the disease it represents.
left: Atrophic epidermis with loss of rete pegs
Acanthotic, hyperplastic epidermis with orthokeratosis and hypergranulosis
Irregular acanthosis with saw-tooth rete ridges and a lichenoid band
checks.expl: These descriptions correspond to the comparison table of the three lichen dermatoses.

checks.q: Lichen simplex chronicus is best understood as:
options: A secondary, reactive process from chronic irritation/pruritus due to an underlying dermatosis
checks.expl: It is a consequence of chronic irritation, often from pruritus arising from an underlying inflammatory dermatosis, rather than a primary disease.

checks.q: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scale is removed) is mechanistically explained by:
options: Thinning of the suprapapillary epidermal plate over dilated dermal capillaries
Loss of the granular layer alone
checks.expl: Removing the scale tears away the thin suprapapillary epidermal layers, disrupting the superficial blood vessels directly beneath.

checks.q: Munro microabscesses are intraspinous collections of neutrophils, while the spongiform pustules of Kogoj are intracorneal.
checks.expl: It is the reverse: Munro microabscesses are intracorneal (stratum corneum), and the spongiform pustules of Kogoj are intraspinous.

checks.q: Match each sexually transmitted ulcer-causing infection with its etiologic agent.
checks.expl: These are the etiologic agents listed in the summary table of vulvar infections.

checks.q: Ancillary testing is generally not necessary to diagnose condyloma acuminatum or molluscum contagiosum.
checks.expl: The summary table lists 'Not necessary' as the ancillary test for both condyloma acuminatum and molluscum contagiosum.

checks.q: 'Donovan bodies,' identified on Warthin-Starry or Gram stain, are characteristic of:
checks.expl: Granuloma inguinale (Klebsiella granulomatis) is diagnosed by culture and Warthin-Starry or Gram stain showing Donovan bodies.

checks.q: Condylomata lata are caused by HPV infection.
checks.expl: Condylomata lata are a manifestation of secondary syphilis; condylomata acuminata are caused by HPV.

checks.q: Koilocytes, the hallmark of HPV cytopathic effect, are characterized by:
options: Enlarged, hyperchromatic, sometimes binucleated cells with smudgy chromatin and perinuclear halos
Plasma cell-rich infiltrate with flat epithelium
Pyknotic nuclei with abundant blue-grey cytoplasm
checks.expl: Koilocytes are enlarged, hyperchromatic, sometimes binucleated cells with smudgy chromatin and clear perinuclear halos.

checks.q: Which statements about condyloma acuminatum are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: Caused by HPV, usually types 6 and 11
Shows verrucous papillae with acanthosis and overlying hyperkeratosis
Koilocytosis may be patchy and focal, confined to the 'valleys' of the epithelium
checks.expl: Condyloma acuminatum does not commonly progress to cancer; the other statements are correct.

checks.q: HSV vulvitis in young women is usually caused by [ blank ], with symptomatic lesions appearing [ blank ] days after sexual contact.
checks.expl: HSV-2 is the usual cause in young women, with symptomatic lesions appearing 3-7 days after contact.

checks.q: About two-thirds of patients with primary HSV infection experience recurrences, which are typically less painful than the primary episode.
checks.expl: Two-thirds of patients suffer recurrences that are less painful than the primary episode.

checks.q: Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusions seen in HSV vulvitis are distinguished by:
checks.expl: Cowdry type A inclusions have a surrounding halo; Cowdry type B inclusions fill the nucleus.

checks.q: Bartholin gland cysts classically occur at the 4 or 8 o'clock position near the vaginal opening.
checks.expl: They are typically located in the labia minora near the vaginal opening, at the 4 or 8 o'clock position.

checks.q: A Bartholin gland cyst most commonly results from:
options: Vulvitis causing obstruction of the excretory duct
Direct HPV infection of the duct
checks.expl: Vulvitis causes obstruction of the excretory duct, leading to accumulation of gland fluid and painful dilation.

checks.q: Which organisms are named as causing infection of a Bartholin cyst/abscess? (Select all that apply.)
checks.expl: Common infectious agents listed are sexually transmitted organisms (chlamydia, gonorrhea) and E. coli.

checks.q: Match each vulvovaginal cyst with its characteristic site/lining.
right: Arises from the periurethral glands; rare
Squamous epithelium; site of prior surgery/trauma
checks.expl: Location plus epithelial lining is the diagnostic key across this group of cysts.

checks.q: Sort each cyst into mucin-secreting or non-mucin-secreting.
checks.expl: The Müllerian/mucous cyst is lined by mucin-secreting columnar cells; Gartner duct and epithelial inclusion cysts are non-mucin-secreting.

checks.q: Hidradenoma papilliferum is the most common benign glandular lesion of the vulva.
checks.expl: It is the most common lesion arising from anogenital mammary-like glands and the most common benign glandular vulvar lesion overall.

checks.q: The defining microscopic feature of hidradenoma papilliferum is:
options: A dual population of columnar eosinophilic (apocrine) cells and clear low cuboidal cells
Sheets of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading
checks.expl: The glands show a dual population: columnar eosinophilic cells and clear cuboidal cells adjacent to the basement membrane.

checks.q: Anogenital mammary-like glands occur along the [ blank ], which explains the occurrence of breast-like glands and lesions on the vulva.
checks.expl: The embryologic milk line, running from axilla to groin, explains breast-like vulvar lesions.

checks.q: The stromal cells of a fibroepithelial (stromal) polyp are estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor positive.
checks.expl: The polyp is a benign, hormonally related lesion with ER/PR-positive stromal cells.

checks.q: A fibroepithelial stromal polyp of the vulva occurs more commonly in which clinical setting?
checks.expl: It occurs in women of reproductive age, more commonly during pregnancy.

checks.q: A biopsy should always be considered for a longstanding, steroid-resistant eczematous vulvar lesion, because it may represent extramammary Paget disease.
checks.expl: Extramammary Paget disease closely mimics an inflammatory process, so biopsy is recommended for steroid-resistant lesions.

checks.q: Secondary extramammary Paget disease is associated with an occult adenocarcinoma from which primary sites? (Select all that apply.)
checks.expl: The lecture lists colorectal, urothelial, ovarian, endometrial, or cervical primaries for secondary Paget disease; breast is not among the five listed sites.

checks.q: In extramammary Paget disease, Paget cells form nests typically located at the [ blank ] of the epidermis, with compression of the basal keratinocytes.
checks.expl: Paget cells are found as nests at the lower epidermis, compressing but preserving the basal keratinocytes.

checks.q: High-grade usual-type VIN (uVIN) represents more than 90% of uVIN cases.
checks.expl: High-grade VIN is the most frequent type, representing more than 90% of uVIN.

checks.q: Up to [ blank ]% of untreated high-grade VIN progresses to squamous cell carcinoma, falling to [ blank ]% if treated.
checks.expl: Up to 9% of untreated high-grade VIN progresses to SCC, falling to 3-4% if treated.

checks.q: p16 immunohistochemistry in usual-type (HPV-associated) VIN characteristically shows:
options: A strong, diffuse 'block' pattern of nuclear (or nuclear/cytoplasmic) staining throughout the epithelium
Staining confined to the basal layer only
checks.expl: uVIN shows p16 positivity in a strong, diffuse 'block' pattern throughout the epithelial layers.

checks.q: Compared with usual-type (HPV-associated) VIN, differentiated-type VIN (dVIN) progresses to invasive carcinoma at a rate of approximately:
options: 32%, with a shorter latency to invasion
9%, with a longer latency to invasion
It does not progress to invasive carcinoma
checks.expl: dVIN is more likely to progress to invasive carcinoma (32%) than usual-type VIN, with a shorter latency period.

checks.q: Which features characterize differentiated-type VIN (dVIN)? (Select all that apply.)
options: Continuous p53 overexpression in the lower epithelial layers
p16 block-positive staining throughout the epithelium
Basal atypia with elongated rete pegs
checks.expl: p16 block positivity and prominent koilocytic change are features of usual-type (HPV-associated) VIN, not dVIN, which is p53-aberrant.

checks.q: Sort each feature into the HPV-associated (usual-type) VIN pathway or the HPV-independent (differentiated-type) VIN pathway.
checks.expl: These features distinguish the two VIN pathways by marker, histology, and age.

checks.q: Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for 90% of all invasive carcinomas of the vulva.
checks.expl: SCC accounts for 90% of all invasive vulvar carcinomas and about 5% of female genital cancers.

checks.q: The most important factor determining lymph node metastasis in vulvar squamous cell carcinoma is:
checks.expl: The most important factor determining outcome overall is lymph node status; depth of invasion is the most important factor determining lymph node metastasis.

checks.q: HPV-associated vulvar SCC occurs at [ blank ] years of age and accounts for about [ blank ]% of vulvar SCC cases.
checks.expl: HPV-associated SCC (about 30% of cases) occurs at 35-65 years.

checks.q: Which histologic patterns are described for vulvar squamous cell carcinoma? (Select all that apply.)
checks.expl: Recognized patterns include keratinizing, non-keratinizing, basaloid, and warty types.

checks.q: HPV-independent (differentiated/simplex) vulvar SCC has a worse prognosis than HPV-associated SCC, despite arising in an older population with a background of a common benign-appearing dermatosis.
checks.expl: This counter-intuitive point is commonly tested: HPV-independent SCC has a worse prognosis than the HPV-associated form.

checks.q: Verrucous carcinoma of the vulva is best described as:
options: An exo-endophytic, well-circumscribed tumor of well-differentiated squamous epithelium with minimal cellular atypia
A poorly differentiated, deeply infiltrative basaloid tumor
A tumor composed exclusively of koilocytic cells
A metastatic deposit from an internal adenocarcinoma

practice.stem: A vulvar biopsy shows acanthosis, papillary growth, and perinuclear vacuolation of squamous cells (image shown). On a cervical biopsy this same perinuclear clearing is a normal glycogenation finding, but in the vulva it should be interpreted as:
options: A normal variant of vulvar epithelium
practice.explanation: Cytoplasmic glycogen and perinuclear vacuoles are largely absent from normal vulvar epithelium (unlike the normally glycogenated cervix); their presence in the vulva, especially with acanthosis and papillary architecture, indicates HPV-related change rather than a normal variant.

practice.stem: The main excretory duct of the Bartholin gland, near its opening into the vestibule, is characteristically lined by which epithelium?
practice.explanation: The main Bartholin duct has a urothelial-type (transitional) lining, sometimes with peripheral mucinous foci; this normal finding can be mistaken for an incidental urothelial contaminant, and cystic change here produces the Bartholin duct/gland cyst.

practice.stem: Together with lichen sclerosus, lichen planus forms the inflammatory background from which which precursor lesion characteristically arises?
practice.explanation: Lichen planus is listed among the premalignant vulvar lesions; together with lichen sclerosus it forms the inflammatory background from which HPV-independent (differentiated) VIN arises.

practice.stem: Approximately what proportion of women with symptomatic lichen sclerosus develop HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma of the vulva?
practice.explanation: Lichen sclerosus is benign, but 1-5% of symptomatic women develop HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma, which is why lifetime surveillance for HPV-independent, p53-mutant VIN is recommended.

practice.stem:
A patient with vulvar psoriasis develops pinpoint bleeding when the overlying silvery scale is removed from a plaque (Auspitz sign). Biopsy (image shown) shows regular psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia with confluent parakeratosis and intracorneal neutrophilic microabscesses.

The Auspitz sign is best explained by which histologic feature?
options: Thinning of the suprapapillary plates overlying dilated capillaries
practice.explanation: In psoriasis the suprapapillary epidermal plates are thinned; removing the overlying scale tears these thin layers and disrupts the underlying dilated superficial dermal capillaries, producing pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign).

practice.stem: In psoriasis, neutrophilic collections within the stratum corneum are termed Munro microabscesses. The analogous neutrophilic collection located within the stratum spinosum (intraspinous) is termed:
practice.explanation: Munro microabscesses (intracorneal) and spongiform pustules of Kogoj (intraspinous) are both neutrophilic collections in psoriasis but occur at different epidermal levels — a frequently confused pair.

practice.stem: Donovan bodies identified on Warthin-Starry or Giemsa stain from an ulcerated vulvar lesion are characteristic of infection with:
practice.explanation: Granuloma inguinale, caused by Klebsiella granulomatis, is diagnosed by culture or Warthin-Starry/Gram stain demonstrating 'Donovan bodies' within an ulcer, as summarized in the lecture's infection table.

practice.stem:
A vulvar biopsy from a patient with painful ulcers showing punched-out centers (image shown) reveals ballooning degeneration of keratinocytes with intranuclear inclusions, some of which fill the entire nucleus.

Which type of viral inclusion fills the entire nucleus in HSV-infected keratinocytes?
practice.explanation: HSV-infected keratinocytes show Cowdry type A inclusions (with a surrounding halo) and Cowdry type B inclusions (filling the entire nucleus), together with marked ballooning degeneration and acantholysis.

practice.stem: The risk of neonatal HSV transmission during vaginal delivery is highest in which clinical scenario?
options: Recurrent HSV with no active lesions at delivery
Active primary HSV infection at the time of delivery
A remote history of HSV more than one year prior
Positive HSV serology without any history of lesions
practice.explanation: There is a high risk of neonatal transmission during vaginal birth, especially with an active primary infection at the time of delivery; recurrences are less severe and reflect established latency in regional nerve ganglia.

practice.stem:
A woman with a prior vulvar surgical scar develops a small, squamous-lined, keratin-filled cyst at the scar site.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.explanation: Epithelial inclusion cysts are lined by squamous epithelium and classically arise at sites of prior surgery or trauma, filled with keratin debris — distinct from the periurethral origin of a Skene cyst or the mucinous lining of a Müllerian cyst.

practice.stem: Microscopically, a fibroepithelial stromal polyp of the vulva typically shows:
options: A central fibrovascular core beneath overlying squamous epithelium
Dense collagenized stroma with small pyknotic nuclei
Uniformly paucicellular stroma with medium-to-large vessels
practice.explanation: The polyp consists of variably cellular stroma with a central fibrovascular core beneath overlying squamous epithelium — distinct from the mesenchymal tumors of Section 7.4, which have different cellularity/vascular patterns.

practice.stem: High-grade HPV-associated (usual-type) VIN typically shows which immunohistochemical staining pattern?
practice.explanation: Usual-type VIN shows strong, diffuse 'block' p16 positivity throughout the epithelial layers, reflecting HPV-driven p16 upregulation, in contrast to the p53-mutant pattern of differentiated VIN.

practice.stem: If left untreated, approximately what proportion of high-grade usual-type VIN progresses to invasive squamous cell carcinoma?
practice.explanation: Up to 9% of high-grade usual-type VIN progresses to SCC if untreated, falling to 3-4% if treated, with about 15% recurrence after treatment — precise, recurrently tested figures.

practice.stem:
A 74-year-old woman with longstanding lichen sclerosus is noted to have an incidental irregularly raised white area. Biopsy (image shown) shows acanthosis, elongated rete pegs, basal atypia, and keratin pearl formation.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.explanation: An incidental raised area within a background of lichen sclerosus, with acanthosis, elongated rete pegs, basal atypia and keratin pearls, is characteristic of differentiated (HPV-independent, p53-aberrant) VIN.

practice.stem: Compared with usual-type VIN, differentiated VIN (dVIN) is characterized by:
options: Younger age at presentation and p16 block positivity
Association with HPV type 16 rather than lichen sclerosus
A higher progression risk to invasive carcinoma with a shorter latency period
practice.explanation: dVIN progresses to invasive carcinoma in about 32% of cases, with a shorter latency period than usual-type VIN (up to 9% untreated) — a counter-intuitive but recurrently tested contrast, since dVIN is often subtle and incidental.

practice.stem: The second most common histologic type of vulvar malignancy, after squamous cell carcinoma, is:
practice.explanation: Melanoma, not basal cell carcinoma, is the second most common vulvar malignancy by histologic type — an easy point to get backwards and a recognised exam trap.

practice.stem: A malignant tumor arising from the Bartholin gland may show which of the following histologic patterns?
practice.explanation: Bartholin gland carcinoma is a recognised, distinct epithelial malignancy of the vulva that may take the form of an adenocarcinoma or an adenoid cystic carcinoma.

practice.stem:
A subcutaneous vulvar nodule is excised. Microscopy (image shown) shows, at low power, numerous capillary-sized vessels with alternating zones of cellularity.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.explanation: Angiomyofibroblastoma is characterized at low power by capillary-sized vessels and alternating zones of cellularity, distinguishing it from cellular angiofibroma (well-circumscribed, uniformly cellular, many vessels) and aggressive angiomyxoma (paucicellular, medium-to-large vessels).

practice.stem:
A biopsy-proven vulvar squamous cell carcinoma measures 1.5 cm in greatest diameter with 1.5 mm depth of stromal invasion.

What FIGO stage does this represent?
practice.explanation: FIGO stage IA requires BOTH a size of ≤2 cm AND ≤1 mm stromal invasion (microinvasive carcinoma). Because the depth of invasion here (1.5 mm) exceeds 1 mm, this is stage IB even though the tumor diameter is ≤2 cm — the IA/IB cutoffs must be applied as a combined rule, not either criterion alone.

practice.stem: A patient with vulvar carcinoma is found to have metastatic disease in the pelvic lymph nodes. This is classified as FIGO stage:
practice.explanation: Pelvic lymph node involvement (and distant metastases) is staged as IVB, not stage III — stage III is defined only by positive inguinofemoral (not pelvic) nodal disease, a very commonly tested trap.

practice.stem: A vulvar carcinoma arising on the clitoris is most likely to drain to which lymph node group(s)?
options: Directly to the pelvic nodes without inguinofemoral involvement
practice.explanation: Midline structures (clitoris, anterior labia minora, fourchette) drain bilaterally, while lateral vulvar lesions drain predominantly to the ipsilateral inguinofemoral nodes; some clitoral lymphatics can also drain directly into the deep inguinal nodes.

practice.stem: Which of the following is an indication for adjuvant pelvic radiotherapy after surgery for vulvar cancer?
options: Disease-free margin of less than 8 mm
A single microscopically positive lymph node with no extracapsular spread
practice.explanation: Postoperative pelvic radiotherapy is required for ≥2 positive lymph nodes, any extracapsular spread (even in just 1 node), or a disease-free margin of less than 8 mm — precise, testable numeric criteria.

practice.stem: A patient is being considered for sentinel lymph node sampling instead of full inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy. Which criterion must be satisfied?
options: Unifocal tumor less than 4 cm, with no clinically suspicious lymph nodes
Clinically palpable, fixed inguinal lymph nodes
practice.explanation: Eligibility for sentinel node sampling requires a unifocal tumor less than 4 cm, with no clinically suspicious lymph nodes — all criteria must be satisfied together; the sentinel node is the first node draining the area of concern, identified with isosulfan blue or radiolabelled technetium.

| Cause | Secondary syphilis (Treponema pallidum) | HPV, usually types 6 and 11 |
| Gross appearance | Flat, minimally elevated lesions | Papillary or flat, single or multiple; may become confluent |
| Microscopy | Dense, predominantly plasma cell-rich mixed inflammatory infiltrate | Marked acanthosis with verrucous papillae, overlying compact ortho-/hyperkeratosis, koilocytes |
| Progression to cancer | Not a premalignant process | Does not commonly progress to cancer |

comparisons.title: HPV-associated (usual-type) VIN vs HPV-independent (differentiated) VIN
comparisons.md:
| Feature | HPV-associated VIN | HPV-independent (differentiated) VIN |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency | Most common | Less common |
| Age | 4th-5th decades | 7th-8th decades |
| Background | High-risk HPV (esp. type 16); smokers, immunocompromised | Lichen sclerosus, lichen planus |
| Gross | Multifocal (>50%), acetowhite papules/plaques | White patches of LS with an irregular raised area |
| Histology | Basaloid or warty; full-thickness atypia | Basal atypia, eosinophilic cells, keratin pearls |
| Marker | p16 block-positive | p53 mutant (aberrant) pattern |
| Progression | Up to 9% untreated | 32%, shorter latency |
| Invasive outcome | HPV-associated SCC | HPV-independent SCC; verrucous carcinoma |

comparisons.title: HPV-associated vs HPV-independent vulvar SCC
comparisons.md:
| Feature | HPV-associated (usual/basaloid/warty) | HPV-independent (differentiated/simplex) |
|---|---|---|
| Proportion / age | ~30%; 35-65 y; premenopausal | ~70%; 55-85 y; postmenopausal |
| Risk factors | HPV 16 > 33 > 18; smoking; immunocompromise | Lichen sclerosus; HPV-independent VIN |
| Gross | Exophytic or ulcerated, often multifocal | Large white exophytic mass with ulceration |
| Histology | Basaloid, warty, (non-)keratinizing | Keratinizing; verrucous carcinoma |
| Prognosis | Better | Worse |

comparisons.title: Vulvovaginal cyst differential (BUG EM)
comparisons.md:
| Cyst (BUG EM) | Site | Lining |
|---|---|---|
| Bartholin | Posterolateral introitus (4/8 o'clock) | Transitional, squamous, or mucinous |
| Urethral (Skene) | Periurethral | From periurethral glands (rare) |
| Gartner duct | Lateral vaginal wall | Low cuboidal, non-mucin-secreting |
| Epithelial inclusion | Site of prior surgery/trauma | Squamous, keratin-filled |
| Müllerian / mucous | Vestibule/vagina | Mucin-secreting columnar |

comparisons.title: Primary vs secondary extramammary Paget disease
comparisons.md:
| Feature | Primary Paget disease | Secondary Paget disease |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Cutaneous — intra-epidermal glandular or pluripotent epidermal/appendageal cells | Non-cutaneous — direct spread or metastasis from an underlying adenocarcinoma |
| Associated primary | None (arises in skin itself) | Colorectal, urothelial, ovarian, endometrial, or cervical adenocarcinoma |
| Clinical implication | Managed as intraepidermal cutaneous disease | Triggers a search for an occult internal adenocarcinoma at the listed sites |

comparisons.title: FIGO staging of vulvar cancer
comparisons.md:
| Stage | Definition |
|---|---|
| I | Limited to the vulva |
| IA | ≤2 cm size and ≤1 mm stromal invasion (microinvasive carcinoma) |
| IB | >2 cm size or >1 mm stromal invasion |
| II | Extension to the lower 1/3 of the vagina, urethra, or anus |
| III | Inguinofemoral lymph nodes positive |
| IVA | Fixed and ulcerated inguinofemoral lymph nodes; or extension to the upper 2/3 of the vagina and urethra |
| IVB | Distant metastases and pelvic lymph nodes |

comparisons.title: Cellular angiofibroma vs angiomyofibroblastoma vs aggressive angiomyxoma
comparisons.md:
| Tumor | Key low-power features |
|---|---|
| Cellular angiofibroma | Well-circumscribed, cellular, many vessels; firm/rubbery subcutaneous nodule |
| Angiomyofibroblastoma | Capillary-sized vessels; alternating cellular zones |
| Aggressive angiomyxoma | Uniformly paucicellular; medium-large vessels evenly dispersed |

comparisons.title: IFLND decision rule for early vulvar cancer
comparisons.md:
| Scenario | IFLND required? |
|---|---|
| Stage Ia, no LVSI | No lymph node dissection required |
| Stage Ia with LVSI, or Stage Ib/II | IFLND required |
| Lateral lesion | Ipsilateral IFLND; contralateral IFLND added only if ipsilateral frozen section is positive |
| Midline lesion (within 1 cm of midline) | Bilateral IFLND |

comparisons.title: Sentinel lymph node frozen-section decision rule
comparisons.md:
| If sentinel node +ve on frozen section | If sentinel node −ve on frozen section |
|---|---|
| Proceed with full IFLND | Omit further dissection (rest of nodes presumed negative) |

Eligibility for sentinel node sampling (instead of full IFLND): unifocal tumor, less than 4 cm, with no clinically suspicious lymph nodes — all three criteria must be met together.

comparisons.title: Bartholin gland/duct complex: component histology
comparisons.md:
| Component | Histology |
|---|---|
| Acini | Mucinous cells, pale (blue-grey) cytoplasm, small bland pyknotic nuclei; densely collagenized stroma |
| Ducts near acini | Flattened epithelium, scant cytoplasm |
| Main duct | Urothelial-type (transitional) epithelium, ± peripheral mucinous foci |

morphology.dx: HPV-related epithelial change (abnormal in the vulva, unlike the normal cervix)

Orthokeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis, and papillary dermal fibrosis with perivascular chronic inflammation

Dense, predominantly plasma cell-rich mixed inflammatory infiltrate in a flat vulvar lesion
Verrucous papillae with acanthosis and koilocytes showing smudgy chromatin and perinuclear halos
Keratinocytes with marked ballooning, secondary acantholysis, and Cowdry type A (haloed) and type B (nucleus-filling) intranuclear inclusions
Cystic dilation of a posterolateral vestibular duct lined by transitional or mucinous epithelium
Cyst in the lateral vaginal wall lined by low cuboidal, non-mucin-secreting epithelium
Dual population of columnar cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and an underlying layer of clear low cuboidal cells
Polypoid lesion with a central fibrovascular core and variably cellular stroma beneath squamous epithelium
Nests of large pale cells located in the lower epidermis, compressing but not destroying the basal keratinocytes

Acanthosis with elongated rete pegs, basal atypia, parakeratosis, enlarged eosinophilic cells with prominent nucleoli, and keratin pearl formation adjacent to lichen sclerosus
Continuous, strongly positive staining confined to the lower epithelial layers with increased positive cells toward the upper epidermis
Irregular, angulated nests of squamous cells infiltrating the dermis in a haphazard fashion with central keratinization

morphology.finding: Exo-endophytic, well-circumscribed papillary proliferation of well-differentiated squamous epithelium with minimal cytologic atypia
